There's a lot more nuance here than most people realize.

Mandates and quotas are illegal. In fact even universities with affirmative action cannot legally create a quota to say '15% green, 20% blue, etc'. The catch is that companies (and public organizations such as universities) can be sued into oblivion for engaging in hiring discrimination. That discrimination is in no way well defined. Is the NBA engaging in discrimination as evidenced by the fact that 74% of their players are black? No. But in fields where merit is a lot harder to show than the NBA, where height/athleticism are trivial to show and demonstrate, companies/organizations are in a way guilty until proven innocent of discrimination.

Another issue is that this sort of lawsuit, regardless of result, would be incredibly damaging to any company that relies on a certain public image and that includes everything from Google to universities. This leads to larger companies and organizations, who would generally be the target of such investigations, going overboard. But even that is beginning to be clamped down on. For instance in 2016 UT: Austin had a judgement upheld by the supreme court only by extreme circumstance. The case was about their use of race as a 'bonus point' in admissions. The final count was 4-3. One justice recused herself and Scalia, who had made scathing remarks about the practice, died before the final decision.

It's fairly certain that any form of employment/academic discrimination on the basis of race (or other issues) will be heard at the supreme court again, and it's likely to be shot down. Anyhow, the point is the current system kind of forces companies between a rock and a hard place. Don't engage in quotas, but if your hiring result doesn't look like a quota get ready to face major lawsuits. And if it does look like a quota, get ready to face lawsuits.

The Carpenters - We've Only Just Begun (1970)

"We've Only Just Begun" is a hit single by Carpenters written by Roger Nichols (music) and Paul Williams (lyrics). Ranked at No. 405 on Rolling Stone magazine's list of "The 500 Greatest Songs of All Time".

The song was originally recorded by Smokey Roberds, a friend of Nichols, under the name "Freddie Allen". It debuted in a wedding-themed television commercial for Crocker National Bank in California in the winter of 1970 with Williams on vocals. Hal Riney, founder of the San Francisco-based advertising agency Hal Riney & Partners, commissioned the song to help Crocker appeal to young people. The song played over footage of a young couple getting married and just starting out. Direct reference to the bank was left out, in part to make the song more marketable. The commercial was very popular and Crocker National's business flourished. Richard Carpenter saw the commercial and guessed correctly that Williams was the vocalist (both of them were under contract to A&M Records). Carpenter ran into Williams on the record company's lot and asked if a full-length version was available. Although it had only two verses and no bridge, Williams stated that there was a bridge and an additional verse, forming a complete song; he and Nichols went on to write them. Carpenter selected the composition for the duo's third single and included it on the LP Close to You.
Released in the late summer of 1970, the single featured Karen's lead vocals and the overdubbed harmonies of both siblings. Following their hit "(They Long to Be) Close to You" onto the charts, "We've Only Just Begun" hit No. 1 on the Cash Box singles chart and No. 2 on the U.S. Billboard Hot 100, becoming the pair's second million-selling gold single. It was considered by both Karen and Richard to be their signature song. According to The Billboard Book of Top 40 Hits (6th edition), on the U.S. Adult Contemporary singles chart, it was the duo's best-performing tune, lasting seven weeks at No. 1 (beating the six-week stay at the top of "Close to You"). The song also helped them to win two Grammy Awards in 1971: for the Best New Artist (The Carpenters) and Best Contemporary Performance by a Duo, Group, or Chorus ("Close to You"). For Williams, the song was a personal victory; it was his first collaboration with Nichols that resulted in a hit single, and it opened the door to many more thereafter. In 1998, the recording was inducted into the Grammy Hall of Fame for recordings "of lasting quality or historical significance".
